The dashboard's Ask button and the Copilot page answer with Gemini when the API service has a key, and offline otherwise (always on the static demo). The key lives only on the server: - Locally: put GEMINIAPIKEY=... in .env at the repo root (git-ignored; see .env.example) and restart the API. - Render: dashboard → stf-live → Environment → set GEMINIAPIKEY (the Blueprint declares it without a value). The model calls the twin's tools (services/api/tools.py) and may state only what they return; the server checks every number in the answer (verify.py) and cites the sources. Each client is rate-limited and the daily caps protect the quota. When a model reaches its limit, the next one answers. Each Gemini model has its own quota, so the server keeps an ordered list and takes a model out for as long as Google's error

says (retryDelay), then tries the next; when every Gemini model is out, a local model (Ollama) answers if one runs, and otherwise the twin's tools answer directly. GET /chat/status shows which models are free. Conversations are kept as JSON documents, one per session (services/api/store.py, under STFDATADIR, default .data/), owned by an anonymous id the browser keeps. Each session carries a context store - the facts the tools established - that whichever model answers next is given, so a hand-over from Gemini to the local model keeps the thread. The store has the shape of a NoSQL one (get / put / delete / list by owner), so MongoDB or Firestore can replace it. On Render's free tier the disk is ephemeral: history lasts until the next deploy. Finding Severity Status S1 POST /command had no authentication. It was reachable through the public ngrok link, so anyone with the link could command the machine. High Fixed. Commands are accepted from the operator's own machine (Host is localhost) or with the operator token STFAPITOKEN (X-STF-Token header). A tunnel is read-only. S2 CORS alloworigins=[""]: any website open in the operator's browser could call the API on localhost (CSRF). High Fixed. An origin allow-list (STFALLOWEDORIGINS), and a foreign Origin is refused for commands even towards localhost. S3 The Vite proxy rewrote Host to 127.0.0.1:8000 (changeOrigin), which made every tunnelled request look local and bypassed S1. Found while verifying S1. High Fixed. changeOrigin: false and xfwd: true. A comment in vite.config.ts says why it must stay that way. S4 The WebSocket had no origin check (cross-site WebSocket hijacking), no client cap and

no message size limit. Medium Fixed. Origin check, 32 clients (STFMAXWSCLIENTS), 1 KB messages, and only {"type": "resync"} is understood. S5 Infrastructure published on every interface: Redis with no password, Postgres with password stf, MQTT anonymous. High (when run) Fixed. Ports bound to 127.0.0.1. Redis and Postgres passwords are required from .env (see .env.example; .env is git-ignored). Mosquitto refuses anonymous clients and uses a password file. S6 The public link served the Vite dev server: source maps, module graph, HMR socket. Medium Fixed. The tunnel now serves the production build (vite preview, port 4173) with security headers. The dev server listens on localhost only. S7 No security headers. Medium Fixed. A strict CSP: scripts from self only (plus wasm-unsafe-eval for the mesh decoder, never unsafe-eval). Also frame-ancestors 'none', nosniff, no-referrer, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy and COOP. The theme pre-paint script moved out

of the HTML so no inline script is needed. S8 Commands validated deep in the runtime only (op a free string, slot unchecked at the boundary). Low Fixed. op is one of a fixed set of four, and slot must match ^[A-C][1-4]$. Anything else gets a 422. Commands are rate-limited per client (token bucket, 4/s, burst 8). S9 torch.load of pickled checkpoints: code execution if a .pt file is replaced. Medium Fixed. weightsonly=True in ml/tune.py and validate.py. S10 The old stack (api/main.py with CORS on 0.0.0.0, the Streamlit dashboard, database/, controller/, hardware/, runall.). It was unmaintained and still runnable. Medium Removed (it is in git history). S11 nanoid < 3.3.18 (dev dependency). High (dev) Fixed (npm audit fix). S12 esbuild ≤ 0.24.2 dev-server advisory (GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99). Replace it with ast.literaleval. High (when run) Designed out. One endpoint on 127.0.0.1, Basic256Sha256 Sign & Encrypt only; user name and password from STFOPCUAUSER / STFOPCUAPASSWORD (12 characters or more), compared in constant time; no anonymous token; client certificates must be in the trust list; every variable read-only. opcua/check.py proves each refusal

against a running server, and a mutant that allows anonymous access is caught. S15 The MQTT broker (Upgrade 14, Sparkplug B and the Unified Namespace) carries the cell's live data and its commands. - tests/testapisecurity.py covers the cases below, and the full suite (100 tests) passes: - local commands are accepted; - commands through a tunnel are refused, but accepted with the token and refused with a wrong one; - a CSRF attempt from a foreign origin is refused; - a DNS-rebinding host name is refused; - malformed operations and slots are rejected; - the rate limiter works; - a WebSocket from a foreign origin is closed, and one from the app's own origin streams. - Against the running system through the public link: - a command gets a 403, and reads get a 200; - the CSP and the other headers are present; - /stf/src/... returns the app shell, not source; - the 3D view (including the WebAssembly decoder) and the live stream work under the CSP.

One HTTP endpoint turns text into speech, trying providers in order until one speaks. The twin's copilot uses it; any other site (a portfolio, a demo page) can use it the same way. The answer is the audio itself (audio/mpeg from ElevenLabs, audio/wav from Gemini and the local voice), with two headers saying who spoke: Header Example X-TTS-Provider elevenlabs, gemini, local X-TTS-Model elevenlabs elevenmultilingualv2, gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts, macOS say GET /chat/tts/status lists the providers and whether each is ready, and the Gemini voices' quota.

Provider Needs Notes ElevenLabs ELEVENLABSAPIKEY (optional ELEVENLABSVOICEID, ELEVENLABSMODEL) MP3. On HTTP 401 / 429 / 503 it is passed over (an hour for a bad key, a minute for a limit). Gemini GEMINIAPIKEY GEMINITTSMODELS in turn: 2.5 Pro TTS (no free-tier quota), 2.5 Flash TTS, 3.8 Flash TTS. Each at its limit is passed over for Google's retry delay. Local macOS (say, afconvert) Offline and free. On Linux, replace LocalVoice with Piper or espeak. Set the order with TTSPROVIDERS, e.g. TTSPROVIDERS=elevenlabs,gemini on a server without the local voice. With none ready the endpoint answers 503 and a browser can fall back to its own speechSynthesis, as the copilot does.
Markdown and [citations] are removed and units are spoken as words ("176 degrees Celsius", "6.16 euros", "O E E"); at most 1 200 characters are spoken, cut at a sentence.

The other site's origin must be in STFALLOWEDORIGINS on the API (requests from other origins are refused), and each client is rate-limited (3 at once, then one every 10 s) under a daily budget (GEMINITTSDAILYLIMIT) - the keys stay on the server. deliberate reset Proven ticks: reach (every hazard zone at least 20 mm inside the guard), fit (no guard part touches a module), logic (every combination of safety inputs checked: motion only with all E-stops released, all doors closed and locked and a reset; any single-channel fault blocks it; a door unlocks only at standstill), air (every cylinder fed only through the safe exhaust valve). Why guard locking, not a light curtain: it removes the need for a measured stopping time. The PL achieved still needs the devices' MTTFd, DCavg and CCF from their datasheets.

Zones Z0-Z5: Z0 hardwired safety (no network), Z1 cell control (the PLC and the four I/O nodes, SL 2), Z2 supervisory, Z3 energy, Z4 DMZ, Z5 enterprise and internet (untrusted). Conduits between zones carry only what is on the allow-list (25 rules for 70 program accesses). Three writable signals the program never uses are flagged. Replay an attack: pick one and compare the outcome with no protection, detection only, and the protected design. Example: a rogue coil write is blocked at conduit C1 because the source is not the PLC (port lock and static ARP). Full page opens the dashboard's security page.

One cookie's journey, as the 3D view plays it and the PLC runs it: One cookie's journey, as the 3D view plays it and the PLC runs it: 1. Retrieve: the crane travels to the mould's slot, lifts, extends the fork, takes the mould and puts it on the belt. 2. Belt and RFID: the belt carries it past RP1 and RP2; the tag is checked against the record. 3. To the oven: the robot picks the cookie off the mould and lays it on the oven tray. 4. Bake in the heated chamber. 5. Turntable, saw, pusher: the oven's gripper moves it to the turntable, which dwells under the saw and turns to the belt; the pusher puts it on the outlet belt. 6. Sort: the sorting line reads its colour and ejects it into its bay. 7. Back

to the rack: the robot collects it from the bay and puts it in a mould at the warehouse belt; the crane stores the mould. The cell overlaps cookies: while one bakes, the crane fetches the next. The PLC's dispatch policy decides what moves next; the one used (reuse) refills an empty mould at the hand-over with a cookie going into the rack. Its full 12-cookie order takes about 425.7 s in the model and 429.8 s when commissioned against the twin. Safety: every transfer takes all its locks at once and in one fixed order, and never starts unless its destination has room, so the cell cannot deadlock. This is proven over every possible completion order.

Every axis is driven by one shared timeline. While an order runs: the crane fetches a mould, the belt carries it to the robot, the robot moves the cookie into the oven, the elements glow and the chamber heats, the oven's own gripper moves it to the turntable, the saw and the pusher work it onto the outlet belt, the sorting line reads its colour and ejects it into its bay, and the robot brings it back to the warehouse. Light barriers flash red while a cookie cuts their beam.

A digital twin of a fischertechnik Smart Tabletop Factory (536634, 24 V) that bakes cookies. One parameter table per module drives the 3D view, the FreeCAD models, the drawings and every analysis, so the CAD, the kinematics and the I/O can never drift apart.

A digital twin of a fischertechnik Smart Tabletop Factory (536634, 24 V) that bakes cookies. One parameter table per module drives the 3D view, the FreeCAD models, the drawings and every analysis, so the CAD, the kinematics and the I/O can never drift apart. Every placement is checked by proofs before it is exported: no two parts intersect in any allowed pose, every part is carried by something, and the workpiece clears every station on its whole journey. Everything is simulated. There is no physical machine connected; the "Live" or "Simulation" chip in the top bar says whether the physics API is running or the twin runs entirely in the browser.

- Warehouse (high-bay warehouse, ft 536631): a 3 x 4 rack (slots A1-C4) and a stacker crane with travel, lift and a telescopic fork (Ausleger); a belt carries moulds to the robot. - Gripper robot (vacuum gripper robot, VGR, ft 536632): a cylindrical robot (swivel, plunge, reach) with a suction cup. It links every station. - Oven (multi-processing station with kiln, ft 536632): tray (Ofenschieber), heated chamber, its own suction gripper, turntable with saw, pusher and an outlet belt. - Sorting line (ft 536633): belt, colour sensor, three pneumatic ejectors and three bays (weiss, rot, blau). Around them: a guard enclosure with doors and E-stops, a PLC cabinet, four remote I/O nodes, a central air station, an edge computer (OPC UA, MQTT Sparkplug, Unified Namespace), drag chains and the wiring.

Exactly 12 cookies exist in the system, each in its own mould. Three flavours, chosen so the colour sensor (which measures reflected brightness, not colour) can tell them apart: Flavour Sensor reading Bay chocolate ~340 mV blau strawberry ~950 mV rot vanilla ~1660 mV weiss Raw dough is pale. A cookie gets its flavour colour when it is baked.
